title: Collective Coherent Perfect Absorption in a Synthetic Photon-Phonon Lattice
authors: Sihan Wang, Qichun Liu, Bo Song, Qiongyi He, Jingwei Zhou, Yulong Liu
abstract: Coherent perfect absorption (CPA) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for controlling classical and quantum light, and has been demonstrated across a broad range of physical platforms. CPA realized in optomechanics relies on interference between the input field and the mechanically scattered field, but is intrinsically confined to the weak-cooperativity regime, resulting in a narrow absorption bandwidth and the mechanical mode remains thermally occupied. Here, we experimentally demonstrate collective interference-induced CPA in a synthetic photon--phonon lattice. By harnessing cavity-reservoir-mediated interactions among Floquet lattice sites, collective interference shifts the CPA condition deep into the high-cooperativity regime. This enables CPA to coexist with ground-state cooling of the mechanical oscillator, together with a broadened non-Lorentzian absorption lineshape and a singular group-delay response. Our results identify collective interference as a route to quantum-compatible perfect absorption and long-lived quantum storage.
summary: The paper reports experimental evidence for collective coherent perfect absorption (C-CPA) in a synthetic photon-phonon lattice. By utilizing long-range interactions, the authors shift the CPA condition into the high-cooperativity regime. This breakthrough allows for quantum-compatible light control, enabling both perfect absorption and ground-state cooling of the mechanical oscillator simultaneously.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving Coherent Perfect Absorption (CPA) in a regime compatible with quantum mechanics, overcoming limitations where conventional optomechanical CPA restricts operation to the weak-cooperativity regime and leaves the mechanical oscillator thermally excited.
main_result: The authors demonstrate collective interference-induced CPA (C-CPA), which shifts the absorption condition into the high-cooperativity regime. This allows for simultaneous ground-state cooling of the mechanical oscillator alongside perfect absorption, enabling long-lived quantum storage.
method: The study uses a Floquet description to model the synthetic photon-phonon lattice and calculates the reflection coefficient by summing over all lattice sites using susceptibilities.
model_or_system: The physical system is a synthetic photon–phonon lattice realized via time-dependent optomechanical couplings, modeled using an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian ($\hat{H}_{	ext{lat}}$) in Floquet space. The interaction involves cavity and mechanical dissipation rates.
key_observables: Reflection coefficient ($R$), group delay response ($	au$), and the effective phonon number ($N_m$).
important_parameters: Cooperativity ($C = 4|G|^2/(\kappa\gamma_m)$), which is tuned to reach the high-cooperativity regime ($C \gg 1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the resonant condition ($\Omega=0$) and assumes operation in the overcoupled regime ($\eta > 1/2$) for efficient lattice excitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of Floquet engineering, the resulting C-CPA curve showing non-Lorentzian absorption, and plots detailing the reflection amplitude and phase evolution across different cooperativities, highlighting the transition to collective absorption at $\Omega=0$.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces CPA and its limitations in standard optomechanics. It then details the theoretical framework using Floquet engineering for the synthetic lattice. The core of the work presents experimental measurements demonstrating C-CPA, showing how high cooperativity enables quantum-compatible absorption features like ground-state cooling and long group delays.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it pushes the boundaries of cavity QED and optomechanics by engineering a platform that achieves fundamental quantum control (ground-state cooling) while simultaneously realizing advanced light manipulation phenomena (CPA).
